utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Ms. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, Your Honours, Aditya Menon, Daniela Kravetz, Priya Gopalan, with our case manager, Line Pedersen; and our legal intern, Elizabeth Herath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. For the Defence starting with Mr. Haradinaj's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ben Emmerson for Mr. Haradinaj together with Rod Dixon, Annie O'Reilly, Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. For Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Gregor Guy-Smith and Chad Mair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. For Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Richard Harvey assisted by Mr. Paul Troop and Mr. Luke Boenisch for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, you may be seated. Just to remind you that you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P191 back up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhahmetaj, you are receiving translation?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And we're going to return now to the minutes of the meeting in Jabllanice on the 23rd of June, at which a co-ordination attempt was made by ascribing names and ranks to individuals in an attempt to improve co-ordination across the zone and to improve links with Jabllanice. And yesterday you told us, first of all, that this was your suggestion, this meeting, in order to improve co-ordination. And you told us that this was the first time you had been to Jabllanice, a place you said that was difficult to reach because of the dangers involved in crossing that terrain and a place which commanders on the western side of the zone would only visit when it was strictly necessary. You recall giving us that evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So if we can just start by looking at the list of names at the top of the minutes, indicating those present. You, I think, are recorded simply as Skenderi in the second line of the typed version and of the Albanian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I don't want us to go through the details of who said what at this meeting because they're there for all to see, but is it fair to say - and you -- first of all, you've seen these minutes, haven't you, they were showed you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's fair to say that this was a discussion in which, as you described earlier on, everybody had their say; correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And decisions were reached by consensus, as they always were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And at the end of the meeting was it agreed that these two sides of the Dukagjin Zone which had been operating really without consultation should now try to come together in some sort of agreed command; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so the question came up, did it not, who would then be chosen, nominally at least, to be the head of this newly formed joint force; is that right? Who would lead it or be its titular or nominal head; did that come up?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is it right that there was really -- there were really two possible candidates. No one suggested that you should be the overall leader, did they, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, or Mr. Qeku or Mr. Tetaj?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no such proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There was some support for the idea that Lahi Brahimaj should be made commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, initially there was a proposal that he be the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you remember who put that proposal forward, from memory?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but if I'm not mistaken it was Rexhep Selimi who proposed him. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And there was also the suggestion that Ramush Haradinaj might take that title; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you remember who suggested that?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the first one to suggest Ramush Haradinaj was Sali Veseli.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then was there a discussion amongst all of you about who might be the best person and a consensus decision reached?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we just, please, look at the very end of each of these documents. It appears on the final page of both the original and the English translation. Well, perhaps I'm wrong, it doesn't appear on the last page of the English translation. It must be -- the list is what I'm concerned with. There we go. It's the bottom half of that English translation and the top half of the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we see there at the very end of that meeting the lists of names that were given, titles that were ascribed to various people?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But looking at that list, I want to suggest to you, it would be completely wrong to infer that from that moment onwards vertical lines of command were established in the way that that list might suggest?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can say that. This was a meeting where proposals were made and names were ascribed to this line of vertical command structure, but there is no decision. This is the minutes that the minute-taker has noted down what was said in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for clarification, sir, I see on the list of people who attended the meeting, I don't see the name of Mr. Lahi Brahimaj, unless maybe I'm making some mistake. Is it correct that he was given this position in absentia?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be able to help there if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I just want the witness to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The name is there, that's why I'm saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He's under a different name, in other words, there's a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's Lahija and Maxhupi appear both at the very beginning of the page, but it is accepted that that is Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That helps me much better. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, that throughout the period that I asked you about from March to September there were no effective vertical lines of command in functioning operation on the ground. That's what you told us yesterday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 23rd of June when the staff was established, there was no such structure. Upon the establishment of the staff and the appointment of people to it, in a way you can consider this as the creation of a vertical line of command at the zone level. However, as I emphasized earlier, the selection and appointment of people at all levels of responsibility was based on their free -- the free will of the people who were appointed. They accepted the responsibilities. There was no order given to them. Everything was done by consensus in the meeting, which is of course a far cry from what you normally do in a normal army, especially appointing commanders at high levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And even after the 23rd of June, it remained the position, did it not, that Ramush Haradinaj did not, for example, issue you with orders?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always proceeded in the same way. The co-ordination and all the activities were carried out in the same way as before the 23rd of June. We discussed together, we analysed the situation, and we took a joint decision, and there was no order to tell people what to do. We evaluated the situation on the basis of what was going on in the ground and notified the people who were responsible for several areas, and we decided jointly, by consensus, and did not give any orders. These were instructions and not orders. And later on, when we had meetings even after the establishment of the structure, we proceeded in the same way. We analysed the situation and acted upon the things that we decided on together. We decided and told people what to do and then we discussed what was done in the next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pausing there for a minute. You've been -- had already been trained within the command structures of a conventional army. I would just like you, please, to explain for the Trial Chamber as shortly and succinctly as you can, perhaps in a sentence or two, what the differences were - just try and encapsulate what the difference was, after the 23rd of June, even after the creation of these theoretical vertical structures, what the differences were between the reality of what was happening on the ground within the KLA in the Dukagjin region and what you would have expected from command responsibility in a conventional army.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there are differences because the organisation of the staff means that there should be orders issued by the staff and then accountability. For example, the commander of the zone is there and there is a deputy commander, and there are people who were responsible for various military areas. That's who will report to the commanders. This is what happens in a conventional army. However, here we have to do only with the beginnings of such a structure. The first attempt to try to create a military structure, and we were hoping that by creating these structures and regular formations we would be able to do something. But we did not have a rules book, we did not have any other regulation. This was just common sense that we followed by -- in creating this kind of command, this kind of staff. The situation was very difficult. We were under a lot of pressure because of the high concentration of Serbian forces in the Dukagjini area. Their presence was far beyond any logical presence that you could expect in those circumstances, and we had to respond to such a situation on the ground and to go a step further, create a vertical command structure, which in the future would be completed and empowered and strengthened and function better in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause there. Pause there for a minute. So what we see on paper here is a blueprint for what might happen at some unspecified point in the future when the structures were sufficiently in place for there to be operational command; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. I would like to give you an example. For instance, I was an anti-armoured artillery --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you. Can you slow down because I think the interpreter is having difficulty keeping up with you and this is rather important. Can you go back to where you said "for example" and you were about to give us an example of your position on this list which I think was in response to my question that this was really a blueprint for some unspecified point in the future. So you were going to say yes, approximately, and you started to say for example. Can you pick it up and speak slowly from there.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will take my case and speak about it. My responsibility was as deputy commander for the anti-armoured unit; however, I could not discharge that responsibility because we did not have the equipment and we were not able to ensure any kind of equipment in order to have anti-armoured units. So this was a blueprint of how we would function in the future. This is a skeleton of the responsibilities that we were going to cover in the future. None of the functions here could be applied and realised in most of the cases. Maybe only the Chief of Staff could discharge his function because he would inspect and have co-ordination between the zones. However, even this was more theoretical than practical. While the other ones that you see here, people who had to do with technical equipment, this was impossible to discharge. If we -- if the situation was -- would be as we expected it to be and we had the equipment and the technique and everything, then we could discharge our functions, but we didn't. So we did not discharge our functions. This is my opinion on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you - with the interpreter's help - do you understand what I mean by the word "aspirational"?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that these were aspirational titles?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, for example, do you know Muhamet Berisha, do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can see he was given the important responsibility of being responsible for chemical and biological defence.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was simply a title with no content, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a position that would require very complex duties to be discharged. I have never seen this person, I don't know him. But a person who is responsible for chemical and biological defence had to be a professional. However, in Kosovo we did not have a lot of professional people in the military area. So we had to use the people that were available in order to organise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that until the 23rd of June meeting you personally had never received an order from Ramush Haradinaj. You were subzone commanders of equal rank even though he was your co-ordinator, you told us yesterday, and you never received an order from him before the 23rd of June. Do you remember telling us that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that and that stands. I told you that everything that was done was done on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just focusing on the question as narrowly as you can for a moment. I'm going to suggest to you that that remained the position after the 23rd of June, that you never received an order from Ramush Haradinaj to do so or not to do anything militarily within your subzone after the 23rd of June.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The subzones and the responsibilities of the subzone commanders continued. We continued to work on functionalising the positions and the responsibilities even after the 23rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in practical terms, after the 23rd of June the relationship between the subzone commanders, in practical terms, remained horizontal?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it remained horizontal in reality, which means that no one could give orders to the other. Everything was done by consensus. It remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So even though in this aspirational blueprint Ramush Haradinaj is listed as commander of the Dukagjin Zone, commanding a chemical weapons unit and so on, the reality on the ground continued after the 23rd of June to be a situation in which each commander operated independently of one another in consultation but without orders being issued. That is a compendious suggestion I would like you to comment on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one comment on that question. It seems to be a little confusing, it refers to Ramush Haradinaj commander of the Dukagjin Zone, commanding a chemical weapons unit, that's how it reads on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's what I said. The point I'm making is these are ludicrous titles. Perhaps I'll put the question a bit more shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to put to you a suggestion, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, and I would like you to agree with it or disagree with it. My suggestion is this, that even though in this document which you've told us was an aspirational blueprint and no more, even though in this document Mr. Haradinaj is listed as commander of the Dukagjin Zone, I suggest to you that the reality on the ground after the 23rd of June remained as it had been before, namely, that the commanders of the various subzones continued to operate independently of each other without orders being issued by anyone, by any one commander. That is my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. As I already explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just to put a little flesh on the bones with a few supplementary questions before I conclude, for example, you never needed to ask Mr. Haradinaj's permission before you sent people over the border to get weapons, did you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need to ask his permission, but I co-operated with him about the way how to go about it. But I didn't need to ask for any permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You didn't need to seek his consent before choosing how and where to deploy volunteers under your command, did you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just as a matter of fact, no suggestion of any criticism at all in any of this, it's just to get the picture straight. But we know that in July a large contingent of soldiers entered Kosovo under the banner of the FARK led by Tahir Zemaj. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And shortly after they entered, they assisted in the battle that took place on the 6th of July in Loxha; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They not only assisted, but they bore the main brunt of that battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, at some point in July, once they became settled - and we'll just have a few words in a moment about how they became settled - but at some point in July is it right that of the seven or eight villages in your subzone, you assigned a number of men, I think 84 in total, to join the FARK soldiers under the command of Tahir Zemaj?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those recruits that I trained and sent to the territory of Albania on their own request was in June, not in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry. So that we're clear, you sent them at their request to join with the group of men under Tahir Zemaj's command who then entered together on the 1st or 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received a letter which requested that we select about 50 recruits from the two villages to complement that unit that would enter Kosova, and this is what I did, I sent the recruits.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just to get -- just to be absolutely clear about this issue of autonomy, all I'm interested in for this purpose is the fact that you're able to make these decisions autonomously, independently. Before you sent those 84 men over the border to join with the FARK forces, you did not consult with Ramush Haradinaj, did you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because as an independent commander in a horizontal structure, you were free to make your own decisions without his approval; is that correct? Without his express approval. He trusted you, but you could make your own decisions.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In short, and I'm just going to summarise it with you now, Mr. Rexhahmetaj, even after the 23rd of June and right up until, let us say, the end of September, even during that period of June, July, August, September, you were dealing with a force made up of volunteers; correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Who could be volunteering for the KLA some of the time and civilians, not engaged at all in the hostilities, at other times; correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And I describe this as a component of territorial defence, which is not very effective but which can help organise defence, because they were ordinary folks. And after doing their shift, they went back home and other people replaced them. So we didn't have military bases to base them. Some of them were with uniforms, some without uniforms. It was a people defending themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so -- and so would you agree with me that one of the reasons why a commander from subzone -- from a particular subzone could not impose his will on another subzone was because everybody was volunteering and everything had to be agreed by consent?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But there was also another reason which you told us about right at the beginning of your testimony yesterday in some detail, which is that these areas, these concentrations, these towns and villages where commanders had been appointed, were fiercely, culturally jealous of their independence from one another. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Another reason why everything had to be done by consensus was because culturally in western Kosovo - as you told us yesterday - these towns, which were concentrations of KLA activity, were fiercely jealous of their independence. They protected their independence from one another. They wouldn't want another leader from another town telling them what to do because that would break the consensus, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct because these people who were appointed were appointed through the will of the local people, going through the rounds I mentioned. So the arrival of everyone else to command, to take over the command, was -- didn't make sense to them. So I think that they wouldn't agree. I believe they wouldn't have liked that, because they trusted us and I believe that we did a good job, given that the objective circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, just to conclude, in your evidence as a whole we've really talked about six subzones, the four that were marked on the map I showed you by Rrustem Tetaj, the one that you've told us about which was on the western side of the road around Voksh, subzone 5, and the zone surrounding Jabllanice which is sometimes referred to as Dushaka -- Dushkaja, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And even after the 23rd of June, right up, let us say, until the end of September, it was not possible, was it, for the commander of any one of those zones to march into another one and tell the people there what to do and what not to do as an order?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless it was asked for, otherwise it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that remains the position despite this aspirational blueprint that we see on the screen in front of us, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rexhahmetaj. I appear on behalf of Lahi Brahimaj, and I just want to ask you a couple of questions in relation to your first contact with him. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was it right that your first contact with him would have been at a meeting in Irzniq on around the 21st of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And at that meeting I believe you have said that Nazmi Brahimaj and Lahi Brahimaj both attended that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Nazmi you describe as having been dressed in a military uniform, whereas Lahi was in civilian clothes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And I believe you also said that Nazmi was the one who did the speaking, effectively, on behalf of Jabllanice and that area; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think you also said - and this is maybe a translation issue - that what we have in English is that you said Nazmi sat in a higher position than Lahi. Does that mean that you were seated in an oda and there was a sort of order in which people sat and that person who sat in the higher order was in the senior position as it seemed to you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were seated according to an order. I think I explained that. Nazmi was in a higher -- seated in a higher position than Lahi, not in the military sense because that was the first time I saw them and I didn't see him after that. I didn't know what position he had, Nazmi or Lahi both. I only spoke in terms of the sitting position in the place where we had the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to misunderstood you. What do you mean by "a higher position"? Was he on a higher chair or a higher cushion or what?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting or the meetings were held in the men's oda. It's a room used specifically for men and everyone sits on a cushion, on a mattress, whereas the guest usually stays at the front. Then come the others according to the distance in terms of kinship or acquaintance. This is how we seat people in our tradition. Even if you are using, let's say, a car, a state -- an official car, usually you sit the guests in the best place, to respect him. Doesn't imply rank, higher rank. We were all equal, seated on the same level. Only the place where one sat, let's say, at the front or on the sides, that made a difference. I don't know if I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I've had the good fortune to visit a number of odas when I've been in Kosovo and because I'm a guest I'm always given a very honoured position. But again, do we understand that what happened on this occasion was that Nazmi appeared to be in a more honoured position than Lahi or a superior position in some way?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting was held in Irzniq. Nazmi came with Lahi from more remote area and because their contacts with other people in our zone were almost non-existent, for that reason I think the host, was Shemsedin Qeku, placed them in a more honoured position. I don't know, because when I entered the room I saw both of them seated. I don't recall it very clearly, but this is how I remember. That must have been the reason. It was the host who decided where everyone would sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. At that stage in your position, did you know whether or not Lahi was a member of the General Staff of the KLA, that's of the overall KLA?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, personally no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In fact, I think it's correct, isn't it, on the 23rd of June at the meeting in Jabllanice, Agron, as he's recorded in the minutes, Rexhep Selimi, as you've corrected identified him to be, he said that Lahi is in fact a member of the central staff, maybe this has been a secret until now. Do you remember that being said in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that he said those words. I only remember that he proposed -- Rexhep Selimi proposed that Lahi be a member. Rexhep Selimi spoke on behalf of the General Staff. This is what I remember. Maybe something else has occurred, but this is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And at that meeting where the minutes record Lahi was appointed as the deputy commander of the Dukagjin Zone, do you from your own knowledge, sir, know that about ten days after that, Ramush Haradinaj issued, first, a warning and then a reprimand to Lahi because he was not fulfilling his duties because he was absenting himself from the zone? Do you have personal knowledge of those matters, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And finally, just this, were you aware that on the 4th of July Ramush Haradinaj issued an order dismissing Lahi as the deputy commander and appointed Nazmi Brahimaj as the deputy commander in his place?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of such an order. I didn't have any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Very well. I have no further questions. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Menon, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you were asked by Mr. Emmerson the following question, and it's in relation to your visit to Gllogjan in April 1998. The question was: "And you went there because you thought it would be a good idea for these village -- various village defences to try to co-ordinate and you wanted to discuss that with Mr. Haradinaj; is that correct?" And the answer which you gave which is at transcript page 1046, lines 20 to 23 was the following: "That is correct, co-ordination was one of the reasons. As I said earlier, we were at the beginning of our organisation. They had more experience than us and we wanted to be ready for any eventuality in case of any Serb attacks." Sir, when you said yesterday that "they had more experience than us," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to Ramush himself and the boys who had overcome a challenge fighting Serb forces. They already had had the first encounter, the first exchange of fire, whereas we were still at the beginning of our organisation. That was why I said "they might have greater experience than us," and I wanted to learn from them. At the same time, I wanted to assure myself that in case of any eventual attack they would provide assistance to us, because we were at the beginning, as I said, of our organisation and we were lying in wait of any potential attack. That was why I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, when you referred to "experience," can you elaborate on any other things that you might be referring to. Are there any other things that you're referring to when you said that "they had experience -- they had greater experience than us"?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained that there they had had the first exchange of fire, and I merely wanted to assure myself that in case of any future attacks they would support us. I think that for anyone who has not tried himself in such a case, in car, wants some support, wants to feel more confident and would be in a better position to co-ordinate our activities to reach the final objective of pan popular mobilisation in war against Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you about something else. The 23 May 1998 meeting about which you gave evidence yesterday, sir, can you tell us who organised that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd May meeting, for that meeting we received an invitation - and I believe that was the case also with other villages - which indicated the venue of the meeting and saying that two representatives from the village should go and attend the meeting that was going to be held on that day at that place. That was the information contained in that invitation that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And from whom did you receive that invitation, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who brought it to the staff, but it said that it came from Gllogjan staff and then it read, as I said, that two representatives from the village are invited to take part in the meeting to be held on that day at that hour, as was specified, along with the place where it was going to be held. That was the content of the invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, at that time who was in charge of the Gllogjan staff?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramush was responsible for Gllogjan, as I was responsible for Isniq [Realtime transcript read in error "Irzniq"]. So we were those responsible for our respective villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Very well, sir. I just want to go back to an answer which you just gave a little while ago in relation to your visit to Gllogjan in April 1998 to visit with Mr. Haradinaj. You indicated - and this is at page 20, lines 22 to 23 - that you wanted to feel more confident and you would be in a better position to co-ordinate our activities to reach the final objective. Can you be a little more specific, sir, as to what activities you wanted to co-ordinate?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence activities for the protection of the villages. After I finished my visit with Ramush, I met Rrustem Tetaj in Lluka before I arrived in my village, in Isniq. So my concern was to meet those people who were elected to lead the war, even though, as I said, we were at the beginning of our organisation of our village self-defence. So I met also Rrustem Tetaj on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But, sir, if you could just be -- perhaps elaborate if you're in a position to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 21, line 17, the answer is recorded relating to a place name "Irzniq" clearly when it must be "Isniq". It's the concern that I warned Your Honours about before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it in context can only be Isniq.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let the witness confirm. Mr. Rexhahmetaj, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not clear what you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you make it clear, sir. Can you see page 21 on your screen. Can you see page 22? Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see page 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Looking up page 22, can you see the number 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see the word, the name of a village just next to the number 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness doesn't speak English and so he can't read what the sentence means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking him to read the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Surely in his context --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That the witness mentioned two villages, in addition to Isniq which is his village, he mentioned also Irzniq.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but we want to know what he mentioned in this specific answer. "Ramush was responsible for Gllogjan, as I was responsible for ..." Yeah, it can only be his home village which I think is said to be Isniq. I don't know how it is pronounced, Isniq.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's a misunderstanding. I met Mr. Haradinaj in Gllogjan and I said that on my way back when I was asked why did -- what kind of co-ordination did you want to discuss? I said that I met Ramush in his quality -- in his capacity as commander of Gllogjan, like I did later, Rrustem Tetaj, Shemsedin Cekaj who was the commander of Irzniq. That is all I said. Ramush I met in Gllogjan together with ten other people, representatives, of Isniq staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess we'll just accept that here you're referring to your own village, whatever it's called. Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you indicated to us that when the KLA headquarters in Jabllanice was requesting fighters from your area to go to Jabllanice, that you discussed this issue with Mr. Haradinaj. Can you tell us why you discussed this issue with Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you please give us the transcript reference and the exact quotation for that question. Could you read the quotation to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sure. I can. Your Honour, if I could just have a minute. I have to pull up yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to wait or can I give an answer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please wait, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's at page 1062, lines 10 through 15, the answer and the question are fairly long so what I'm going to do is I'm going to read an excerpt of that and if Mr. Emmerson has an objection then he can make the objection after I've read it out. "Any kind of request not only requests not only supporting with firepower but any other request. This is a time when we were teaching other people how to communicate within the military structures, and I discussed this with Ramush and I insisted to have some sort of communication so that requests coming from Jabllanice or any other place should be co-ordinated" --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As the transcript shows, that is not the question that Mr. Menon put and the assumption of Mr. Menon's question was incorrect [Microphone not activated] ... perhaps to rephrase it accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, I can rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, in June of 1998, do you recall having discussed any issues of -- involving Jabllanice, the KLA headquarters there, with Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I insisted that we needed to have contact with that part because it was cut off geographically and it was a remote area. And this request for meeting and co-ordination was made because we had divided the responsibilities for the subzones. And at that time there was a request made by Jabllanice in the village of Rashiq, which is part of subzone 4, to send some fighters in order to support the front line there. Later on the members of the Rashiq staff came to me and told me that there was a request made by Jabllanice to send fighters there. And I postponed their sending -- the sending of these fighters there. I met Ramush. I discussed the issue with him and I said that it is -- it makes sense militarily that if there is a request by another area or a zone for fighters and fire support, the commander needs to know whether they can be sent, if that is possible to be done, and that was the reason why I discussed this with him. If help is required, we need to cover the various areas and the responsible people for the subzones need to know what happens within their area of responsibility. This was the reason why I insisted that we needed to have more contact with Jabllanice. At that time those areas were also under threat and under attack. This is the main reason why I did that and why I requesting that meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, the village that you referred to as Rashiq, can you just spell that for us, that village, how is that village spelled?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: R-a-s-h-i-q.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. My question to you now, sir, is: Why did you approach Mr. Haradinaj on this particular issue of Jabllanice having sought reinforcements from Rashiq?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I didn't know anybody else there. I had never been to Jabllanice. And simply, I just discussed this issue with him. What were the possibilities of having such a meeting or having contacts with them, because I had information that he had family ties with Jabllanice. And I thought that through him -- or maybe not through him but we could sit together and co-ordinate activities. Because this was to the benefit of a better organisation and co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "he had family ties with Jabllanice," can you elaborate on what family ties he had with Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the information I have, I think Lahi is Ramush's maternal uncle. I have said this in the statement as well and in our areas there are not too many people living there, so people know each other and the family ties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Menon really needs to take time about this. There is no dispute about this and never has been. Of course there's a family relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In any case, the witness is also not disputing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just simply developing the answer that had been given on the record so that the record is clear for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, how -- once you had this discussion with Mr. Haradinaj, how Mr. Haradinaj communicated your concerns to those in Jabllanice, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but when I received this request I was told by him that: I will find a way to have such a meeting, but I don't know anything further than that, what he did. And I insisted, I told him that it would be best if we had some kind of co-ordination and to know how we could support each other. This was an organisational issue and an issue of reciprocal support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you confirm for us because you indicated that what Mr. Haradinaj said is that he would have find a way to have such a meeting. Can you just confirm to us that in fact there was such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, some time passed before we had that, maybe two weeks or so, and I was notified that we would go and have a meeting in Jabllanice. And then there was this idea and proposal that the organisational structures should be advanced at the zone level. So it was on the same date that the skeleton of the operational staff of the Dukagjini Zone was created, as I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Just so we're clear on the dates, when did you approach Mr. Haradinaj about this particular issue involving Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But perhaps a month and a year, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I approached him about two weeks earlier than the date of the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, then, sir, can you confirm for us what the date of that meeting was then?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of the meeting was the 23rd of June, when we formed the vertical structure for the Dukagjini Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that -- I've just been notified, Your Honour, that it might be a good time for a break because it is 3.30 and I was just about to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Menon. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have the witness enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. May the witness please come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In the meantime I would ask, actually, that Exhibit P297 be called up, which is the witness's statement of 24th of September, 2010. If we could go to page 6 in the Albanian version and page 4 in the English version and only the Albanian should be shown to the witness. In addition to that, Your Honour, we have distributed hard copies of the list of corrections which the witness had made to his statements and which is admitted as Exhibit P299. If we could scroll up in the Albanian version a little bit as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Excuse me, scroll down. And if the witness could be handed a hard copy of the list of corrections which he made to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to direct your attention to paragraph 18 and I'd like you to read -- it's on the screen in front of you first, sir. If you could look at the document on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So I want to direct your attention to paragraph 18. If you could just read the first four sentences of that paragraph which appear in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, the first four paragraphs [sic] also appear on the English version page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And that's the first four sentences of paragraph 18, sir, that you read? Because I misspoke. I think I referred to the word "paragraph" instead of "sentence." So have you read the first four sentences of paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have the document in front of you. Can you go to the third page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for your reference it's also the third page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of which document, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's the hard copy document that Your Honours have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And these are the list of corrections to the statement. And I would direct Your Honours' and the witness's attention to paragraph 3, letter (e) which refers to paragraph 18 of the statement which is on the -- which is on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, can you read -- can you read that to yourself? It's paragraph 3, letter (e), which are the corrections that you made to paragraph 18 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read the correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: To yourself, yes, to yourself.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You read it. Okay. I have a question for you, sir. It relates to the second bullet point under paragraph 18 where you say: "The fourth sentence of the Albanian version of my statement should correspond to the English version, which reads, 'Prior to 23 June ... he already had de facto authority over the Dukagjin zone.'" And I don't think there's any dispute that the "he" you're referring to is Ramush Haradinaj. Can you tell me, sir, what you meant by the word "authority"?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that based on the resistance that he put up with his family, the incident had a lot of echo in the whole country and Ramush as a result of that was widely respected for this resistance that he put up in protecting his family and his village. And with the passage of time, in fact, he became famous. Everyone -- most of the people knew him and had a lot of respect for him, because, as I said, he put up that resistance and protected his family and his village. This is my way of thinking when I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir -- I'm sorry, sir, continue.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on the basis of what I just said, people respected him and in -- if you are respected you enjoy authority. I'm -- I don't mean here legal authority, but the authority of a person who was successful in protecting his family and his village and his people. This is my line of thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us whether KLA soldiers in the Dukagjin Zone respected Ramush Haradinaj's authority? A.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So long as it's clear that the question is being put with the meaning of the word "authority" as the witness has just defined it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- then in other words that he's a respected individual. There's a very great risk of the transcript appearing with a misleading question and answer, as Mr. Menon well knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply -- I'm simply -- the question is based upon what is in the witness's statement, so he refers to the fact -- he refers -- let me finish. He refers to the word "authority" in his statement. He's explained what that word means in the -- in -- before Your Honours. And I'm simply asking him to elaborate on that by asking specifically whether that would apply to the KLA soldiers in the Dukagjin Zone, whether they shared that same impression of Ramush Haradinaj, as the witness has indicated in his statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, again, Mr. Menon skillfully but misleadingly elides what is in the statement with what is the explanation. The witness has explained that when he used those terms in his statement what he meant was that Mr. Haradinaj was respected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have heard that, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are going to have a prolonged argument about this, I think it would be better for the witness to be excused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, just carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat the question for you. Can you tell us whether KLA soldiers in the Dukagjin Zone respected Ramush Haradinaj's authority, and I'm referring to the time period from prior to the 23rd of May, 1998, and after the 23rd of May, 1998 -- or, excuse me, after the 23rd of June, 1998, it should read.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population always respected him. The population was suffering, ordinary people were suffering, and he defended them. So that's why they respected him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And my question actually was specific to KLA soldiers, sir.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole population --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- wanted defence and they got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. And can you elaborate for us, sir, on why Mr. Haradinaj was appointed as the commander of the Dukagjin Zone officially on the 23rd of June, 1998? Why was he selected?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we proposed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But why did you propose him?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we were not sure that we, the others, could carry that duty upon our shoulders. That's why we proposed him. He had shown what he could do and we proposed him. Ramush could have refused, but he took on the responsibility by respecting us and our proposal. He, out of his goodwill, he accepted the task, but he could have refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "he had shown what he could do," can you clarify what you mean by that, sir.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned it earlier. He had shown that he was a good soldier, a good leader, and a person who could gather people around him; and that's why we decided that Ramush be a co-ordinator for the subzones earlier. The same logic worked later. There were five professional officers there and each of us could have taken that burden upon their shoulders, but we proposed him and he did not hesitate. He respected our will and our proposal for him to be the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say that Ramush Haradinaj was a person who could gather people around him, what do you mean by that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that he knew how to respect other people, he was a good communicator, he was reasonable. So this was a person who could gather people around himself. It was this that I meant. He was able to discuss the problems that people had with them. He listened to their concerns, and that's why he had that reputation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And earlier on, sir, you indicated - and this is at transcript page 33, line 7 - you had indicated that -- and this is in -- this is in reference to yourself and the other commanders that: "Perhaps we were not sure that we, the others, could carry that duty upon our shoulders." Can you elaborate on why you and the other commanders felt you couldn't carry the responsibility on your shoulders?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it was only a supposition because we -- because we had already scored some results, but I know very well from my own experience that it was not an easy task. I said even earlier that we based our proposal on his abilities, his qualities, which he had displayed earlier. That's why we proposed him to be in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us whether Ramush Haradinaj was a professional soldier at that time?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not a professional soldier, at least not to my knowledge. I only -- I know that he had only done his military service, but as time showed one may be born to be good at something, maybe an inherent quality, because you have cases of professional soldiers who are not very successful in their careers. I think it's a personal quality that one may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us why you -- why specifically you and the other professional soldiers proposed Ramush Haradinaj for leadership of the Dukagjin Zone?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. Can you tell us why you and the other professional soldiers proposed Ramush Haradinaj for leadership of the Dukagjin Zone on the 23rd of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we respected him and we could stand by him professionally as soldiers, we could help him. I already explained earlier that the people admired him and this was one more reason that prompted us to propose him to be in that leading position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhahmetaj, I just wanted to clarify one little point with you. Before I clarify it, I want you to confirm that I heard you properly this afternoon when you were being asked questions by Mr. Emmerson, did I hear correctly that you said you do not know Muhamet Berisha and you have not seen him?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I never saw him, but I don't recall to have met him. Maybe if I see him today I might recognise him. Because in those circumstances when we met it was a war time and there were many people I don't know, didn't recognise. But with the passage of time I started to get to know more people. Sometimes in my own village there was someone I didn't know. Then after a long time because I went to study in the military academy and left the village. So there were many people in my own village that I didn't know, but when I returned gradually I got to know them. So the name doesn't ring a bell, but if I see him by sight maybe I will remember -- I will remember who he is. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't remember seeing him at the meeting of the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name, as I said, doesn't tell me anything. But I wanted to explain something about people being present there. Naim Maloku --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about him. You don't remember seeing him at the meeting --

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were several people, people, I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... listen to my question, Mr. Rexhahmetaj. Don't you remember seeing him at the meeting of the 23rd, just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember to have seen him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible that he could have been present but you don't know or ... ?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER Rexhahmetaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's possible then I can't take the matter any further. Thank you so much. Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench? Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rexhahmetaj. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You may stand down and you may travel well back home. You are excused. You may stand down. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there are some scheduling issues to discuss and I'm going to pass the microphone over to Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have any witness for the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: We do not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, I know that Mr. Emmerson had asked that we talk about the way forward today. Good afternoon, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm very happy for Mr. Rogers to start in the sense that he has more information than I do, but I know that we -- the schedule is shifting and the concern that I have is that I think it unlikely that we will have sufficient evidence to use up the two-week schedule that is listed at the end of next -- at the end of this month, but I see Mr. Rogers may have more up-to-date information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let Mr. Rogers tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I'll just adjust the volume on the headset. Your Honours, the next sitting schedule is 26 September to 7 October inclusive and we're due to file the precise order of witnesses on the 12th of September and we will do that. But presently we have four witnesses scheduled for that period of time based upon the progress of the hearing we've had so far. They are Witness 3, Witness 77, and two 92 ter witnesses, one is, I anticipate, relatively short, Mr. Togal and Witness 76. There was also the question, of course, as to what we may do with Witness 75, and it may be that that time could be used to finish that witness, depending upon where we are with the various applications and disclosure. And also we have the question of what we do with Witness 80, and I'll turn to that in closed -- private session in a moment, if I may. Can I just also mention one thing which affects perhaps not the next sitting schedule but the one after, which is the ruling that we await from Your Honours in relation to 89(F) because we need -- we sort of need to know where we may be with that before we think about the next set of witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We just missed the filing time this afternoon. You'll get it on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm grateful. That deals with that. Then we will know where we are and we can be looking at what impact that may have on the future schedule. Your Honours, as Witness 3 is a live witness pursuant to Your Honours' order, we think that he will take some while as a crime base witness to explain his story and for him to be further examined as necessary and also Witness 77 we anticipate will take some while based upon the current progress, as he's also dealing live with some events. And probably a little bit with Mr. Togal, I don't know quite how much with him. And Witness 76 could also be of some length, bearing in mind Witness 75 in terms of subject. So we think we probably will use most of the next two-week time up, depending upon my learned friends' cross-examination, of course. It may be that we're a little bit shorter on that. I see Mr. Emmerson shaking his head, but to some extent I'm in their hands because I don't know how far they anticipate going with witnesses and even when they anticipate being short they are understandable reasons longer. But that's our understanding. Can I mention Witness 80 whilst we're having the discussion and perhaps we can just go into private session and then we can have a full discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I foresee that we will probably use no more than four court days in the next session unless Witness 80 is called court, and I think it right to bring that to your attention. The situation is this: Just going through the witnesses - and I leave aside the possibility that there may be movement in relation to Witness 80 which results in him being called and were that the case, then a very large of the session will be taken up in relation to his evidence potentially. But if his evidence is not to be adduced during the next sitting session and I think Mr. Rogers thinks that is, on balance, unlikely, we are left with this situation: Potentially we have the remainder of Witness 75. We then have Witness 76, who is very brief indeed. Witness Togal, who is momentary and may well not be called. There's still an issue to be decided, but a momentary witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's my issue and he will be a momentary witness, but it will be momentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, I mean, we're talking ten minutes. Witness 77 is a significant witness, it may take us a day, it's possible. And that leaves Witness 3. Even if Witness 3's testimony is given in full afresh, it took I think a day -- a little over a day on the last occasion, so you've in total got about three days there. Now, the reality of Witness 3 is this, we have consented to the Prosecution's application under 92 ter that his testimony and transcripts from the previous trial - and this is a consent that has come from all accused - be admitted. The Prosecution's position, stated position, in their opening brief at paragraph 14 -- I'm sorry, it's their 92 ter motion that I'm looking at paragraph 14, they're stated position is that the only additional evidence that they wish to elicit orally is as follows: [As read] "Witness 3 will be examined," and that is examined orally, "about accusations he heard being levelled against a Catholic man whom the Prosecution will argue is Pal Krasniqi with whom Witness 3 was detained." In other words, the only oral testimony that the Prosecution sought to elicit live from that witness is the fact that he heard accusations being levelled against a co -- an alleged co-detainee. Well, one can imagine how long that will be likely to elicit, minutes one would think. Now, the position is contrary to the Prosecution's 92 ter application and contrary to the position that has been taken by the Defence, the Trial Chamber issued a ruling that because the witness's testimony concerns the act and conduct of the accused, he needs to give his testimony orally. But that is not the position that either party is seeking. The position of the Prosecution is they wish to ask him one or two additional questions. The position of the Defence is that that is perfectly acceptable, providing his full testimony, 92 ter, and transcript from the previous trial is admitted. The Prosecution would, no doubt, wish to have that happen as well because, clearly, we don't want to hear all over again evidence that's been fully cross-examined. So the reality with witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Is it the position of all three Defence teams that -- just sit down, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I thought you were asking for a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. Is the position of all three Defence teams that they don't even intend to cross-examine him on the oral part that the Prosecution wants to lead him?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, no. Insofar as the Prosecution has indicated in its 92 ter mediation that it has certain additional questions to ask him, it may well be that -- I won't be asking many questions about it because it's nothing to do with my client but it may well be that there be questions asked by other counsel in relation to that minute's worth or five-minutes' worth of additional evidence. But the critical point is it's a monumental waste of this Tribunal's time and resources to hear afresh the whole story --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you and I'm trying to make sure that we don't waste that time. That's why I want to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- with other counsel. Mr. Guy-Smith, is it Mr. Balaj's Defence's position that they do not intend to cross-examine this witness on the oral testimony that this witness is going to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The oral testimony that was just discussed with you and Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is a correct statement. I do not intend to cross-examine him on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence that has been given so far, absolutely no intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's not the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, let me come to it. We don't know what additional questions are going to be asked of this witness. It seems to me that the most sensible course for the Prosecution to take is to go, take a statement from the witness on the further matters, whatever they may be, that the Prosecution wishes to adduce, provide a copy of that statement to the Defence, and then we can tell you yes or no whether we wish that witness to be called to be questioned about those additional matters. We don't know what they want to ask. I can tell you as I stand here that I may have a very few questions because this will apparently relate to matters that occurred in Jabllanice, which are laid at the door of my client by the Prosecution in this case. To that extent, I may have a few questions. I will not be detaining the Court long, and that's why I propose that the solution that I do that the Prosecution proceed in the normal way, go take an extra statement, give us a copy of it and we will tell you whether we need them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I know you are on your feet, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to say obviously the critical point is that at the moment, on Your Honours' ruling, the Prosecution are required to elicit testimony live all over again and no one's asking for that. The Prosecution have asked -- no, I'm sorry, none of the parties are asking you to order that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But that being the position, it is agreed by consent that, whatever happens, his 92 ter statement which was admitted on the last occasion and his testimony which was admitted on the last occasion will be sought to be introduced before the Trial Chamber. Now, if the Trial Chamber thinks it a profitable use of time to have him tell the story all over again, then obviously that's a matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what happens when a 92 ter witness comes. Can I just confirm something with the Prosecution because I hear what you are -- what you want and I would like to make sure that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I might and it may be of some insistence with regard to your inquiry. We have a supplemental information sheet dated the 24th of January, 2011, which deals with the specific issues that we're talking about right now. And that seems to be pretty clear about what the level of inquiry is. So I think the matter can be addressed if everybody, meaning the Defence or Mr. Harvey and the Prosecution, agree that that's what we're talking about. We're talking about literally moments of time here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, Mr. Harvey is suggesting that you could take a statement from the witness on the further oral testimony you intend leading, and Mr. Guy-Smith is referring to some document of the 24th of January, 2011. First of all, is it possible, within the capacities of your office, to get the statement before the witness is due to come and give it to the parties on that little part that you want to lead him about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it would be difficult to obtain it. We can endeavour to obtain a further statement relating to issues that we would wish to cover, but I think it will be difficult. Normally we wish to have the witness and see the witness in person, but given his present location which is known -- obviously I'm not going to explain where it is, but I know that will be very difficult if not impossible to do between now and the next sitting period. I can't explain why, but it will be. The other thing is of course -- and I can't refer to it in open session, but I'm reminded of Your Honours' decision and it was Your Honours that wished to hear the witness and refused the application of the Prosecution. And we're very willing and able and entirely content to place before you a witness that was present, that can explain in detail about exactly what happened to him and the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't go there. I understand that the Chamber might have called him, but I also do understand that a 92 ter witness does not have to spend ten minutes in court. So we are -- even if he comes here, strictly speaking, the 92 ter part of it shouldn't take more than is necessary. You're going to ask him: Is this what you would say if you were asked to answer questions? Yes. Then you tender the statement. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: If he was a 92 ter witness, yes, but he isn't because Your Honours have refused the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, is this on your part an application for reconsideration of the ruling on this?
