utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I suppose in effect it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There being no objection in relation to it. Obviously he can be here and if the Chamber has specific questions to put to him or Mr. Rogers wants to put supplementary questions to him then that can be done. But given that the overarching duty on the Tribunal is to ensure efficient management of time, given that neither of the parties are requiring this witness to tell his story all over again because he's been fully cross-examined on it once before and given that the Prosecution has only a very limited amount of additional examination on which the parties can then ask questions, if necessary, it's simply a scheduling issue. It's a massive waste of your time and of money for the witness to give his evidence all over again when he can be here and not be asked any specific questions, but from a point of view of timing on that basis he would be in and out in a session. He's certainly not going to take a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If he would be 92 ter'd, would there be a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Not on what's gone before, only on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, that's what I mean. On the fresh evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: None of us wish to cross-examine him on what went before. It's all on the record. He's been fully cross-examined already.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I shook my head in response to your question and I shook my head side to side which would be affirmative. No, there's not any intention on the part of us to re-cross-examine on what's gone before, none whatsoever, as a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And is this general strategy? I mean, not -- 92 ter witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, it's as regards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- this particular witness. And the Chamber has already admitted a fair number of witnesses in this fashion already where there is essentially the record that you have from the previous trial with full cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, gentlemen, you can't all speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- Can I just indicate, in case Your Honours should be under any misapprehension and unless I'm mistaken, this is the only witness in the category of somebody who gave evidence at the last trial, was cross-examined in full, and is coming before this Tribunal, again, in person. There are a large number of witnesses who gave evidence at the first trial and were cross-examined in full where the whole of their evidence is going into the record, but the only reason why this witness falls into a different category from the others, in other words, the only reason it wasn't just admitted by consent, is because the Prosecution wishes to ask a few additional questions. So the logic of the situation dictates that the witness arrive here with or without a statement but certainly with the proofing notes which indicate what it is that the Prosecution wishes to elicit from him but that is easily achievable by the time he comes into the witness box. He attests in the normal way to his testimony and his transcript. No party on this side of the court wishes to cross-examine him on that material. The only questions that will be put to him are by the Prosecution on the very limited basis they have given notice of and by the Defence in relation to any of those issues. Now, on the issues that the Prosecution has so far given notice of, I have no questions, Mr. Guy-Smith has no questions, Mr. Harvey may. But on any view, this man will be in and out, if it's done properly and efficiently, in an hour at most. So just looking back at our schedule, if Witness 80 isn't going to be here we've effectively got one witness who is substantial and may last a day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, before you go to the next witness, the questions I was asking earlier I was anticipating what you just said to Mr. -- to Judge Delvoie --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That you are effectively asking for a reconsideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I suppose that's what it comes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm trying to find out whether in fact we can resolve that if you can just put it formally, but it does seem as, because of Mr. Harvey's position, it becomes difficult to reconsider.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because of Mr. Harvey's position ... ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where he says he may very well have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no, I think you may have misunderstood him. He said he may very well have questions about the new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I mean. You don't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I give way to him to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Let me make matters clearer. There is nothing even in the new material of which we have been given notice back in January that involves me needing to ask a single question. I apologise I had not refreshed my memory about that new material before the subject came up, I looked at it again. I cannot see the basis on which I would be asking a further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In that case, I join in the application I think Mr. Emmerson is just about to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. That makes it much easier. Mr. Emmerson, are you making the application, by reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber doesn't have a very sharp recollection of this motion --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- where the Prosecution, probably jointly with you, agreed that this evidence goes in. We'd just like to look at our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we take a break and come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, if I could just indicate, Your Honours will recall, for example, Zoran Stijovic. Your Honours will recall we've heard the testimony, briefly, of Zoran Stijovic. We've heard the testimony, briefly, of Bislim Zyrapi. Both of those witnesses gave evidence in the previous trial and in both cases they were called in this trial in order to adopt their testimony and give a little bit more, and answer some questions about the little bit more. Witness 6 and Witness 3 were both witnesses on the Prosecution's 92 ter application, both of whom concerned detailed events alleged to have occurred at Jabllanice, and both of them in effect cross-relating, it is said, to the same sequence of events. Your Honours have admitted, by agreement, Witness 6 under Rule 92 ter -- I'm sorry ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I had misunderstood that. Apparently there's an -- it's outstanding. The point remains the same, though, that it's only if the Prosecution want to elicit additional testimony that it is necessary for the witness to attend to give it and they really should only give the additional testimony or any clarification that's absolutely required. And that is certainly a -- the workable position as regards -- as regards Witness 3 because we remain of the position that none of us wishes to re-open what took place before, but obviously if the Prosecution want additional material then they must be entitled to have it and if questions arise they must be asked. But it would be -- it is inevitable that Your Honours are going to be faced with the admission of the transcript and the 92 ter statement one way or the other of that witness, and it would, as I say, just be a monumental waste of the Tribunal's time and money to have a day of taking the evidence all over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we then take a short break and we'll call you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 4.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the indulgence. The Chamber has considered this matter and it does want to hear the witness, so your application for reconsideration will be denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I nonetheless indicate to Your Honours just take stock of where that leaves us. Going on the length of time that Witness 3 was giving his testimony in full on the last occasion, that would occupy just a little over one day of the Tribunal's time. A similar period of time can be expected in relation to Witness 77. So that would take us maximum two and a half or if one stretches it for procedural difficulties to three days. We then have cross-examination outstanding for Witness 75, let us say the maximum would be a day, and momentary evidence from Witness 76 and Witness Togal under 92 ter. There is -- it is inconceivable that we will occupy more than one week of the Tribunal's time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I have a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I just -- unless Your Honours want to say something, could I finish the sentence that I was going to complete. I simply wanted to say to Your Honours and for the purposes of the Tribunal's time since we are alternating with Judge Hall and Judge Delvoie in the Stanisic case, it strikes me that the best and, as a matter for trial management, of course, and I don't know how the Stanisic case would be affected but if we are not going to be using the second week because there's not enough evidence to use that second week, then that obviously is a week that is available in one way or another for the Stanisic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. But maybe on Monday when you see the decision on 89(F) you may very well consider that there may be work for us to do. Are there any other issues that the parties would like to raise? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No. Just to thank Your Honours for the decisions in the two matters relating to the orders that have just been released. I will do the best I can to advance that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So I can deal with that. Your Honours, I don't know how a -- how we -- sorry, let me start again. I don't know how quickly we may be able to bring other individuals in respect of the 89(F) witnesses. I am anticipating from Your Honour's indication we might need to be looking for some time to fill with them. And I suspect that by speaking to my learned friends we may be able to resolve some of those issues as well because I know what their discrete concerns were about them and it may be that they're resolved, but we'll see. I don't share my learned friends' confidence that on the current running schedule and the way things have been progressing so far that the witnesses that we've already have identified will take as little time as suggested, but I'm not hearing Your Honours vacating any of the sitting time, so there's little more I think I need to say at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, we don't intend to vacate any of the time until we see actual need on the ground that there is a need for that. Okay. Anything from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simply this, Mr. Rogers will have to file the actual list of witnesses he proposes to call in the next session by the 12th. Would Your Honours therefore immediately upon the filing of that invite the Registry to seek submissions of the parties as to what the position is time-wise because obviously we could -- Your Honours will want to reconsider the situation in relation to sitting times once we know who is actually going to be called. I mean, Your Honour has just indicated that there may be additional witnesses arising out of the 89(F) ruling. Well, if Mr. Rogers is not a position to call them in the next session -- I'm standing here trying to assist the Tribunal efficiently to manage its time. I could see we could very well end up in a situation where what is time that could be being used for sitting either on this or the other case is not going to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you can rest assured, Mr. Emmerson, that the Chamber shares that concern. But at the same time the Chamber does want to make sure that all the evidence and every important evidence is placed before it for its own consideration. So yes, we still have to have a fair trial and the fair trial considerations weigh a little more than expeditiousness, I think, if not much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would never question that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much for not questioning that. From the way I see Mr. Guy-Smith sitting, it doesn't look like he has got anything to raise this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do not. I trust you will have a good weekend -- I'm sorry, I trust you will have a good period of time until we see each other next. One of you I know I'll be seeing sooner than later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Same to you, Mr. Guy-Smith. And Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I join in wishing you all a pleasant respite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to you too, Mr. Harvey. We take an adjournment and come back on the 26th of September at --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I think it's 9.00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 9.00? Courtroom 1. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
